---
order: 1
unit: trail
title: A day's trail
summary: "Everyday things online leave a trail: a message, a photo, a game score, a search, a place you checked in. Most of it is fine. Some of it is worth a second thought, because it is hard to take back, says where you are, or is about someone else. A trail is not something to fear; it is something to notice."
language: science
shape: 5e
hook: "Kai's Saturday: a game, a video, a photo of the dog, a message to Nan, a search for pancake recipes. Which of these could still be around next year?"
---
Kai is made up, and so is everything Kai does here. Nobody has to say what they do online.

## Engage: what stays?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to a guess first: most of what we do online is kept somewhere, even when it disappears from our own screen."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Kai sends a funny photo of the dog to a group chat, then deletes it a minute later. Is it gone?"
  options: ["Maybe not: someone may have seen it, saved it or taken a screenshot", "Yes: deleting takes it back from everyone", "Yes, if Kai deletes it within a minute"]
  actual: "Maybe not. Deleting takes it off Kai's screen. Anyone who saw it in that minute could have saved it, and the chat app may keep a copy for a while."
```

## Explore: Kai's Saturday

```step
stage: run
insight: "Sorting a day of ordinary actions shows that most of a trail is fine, and that a few things are worth a second thought."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Here is Kai's Saturday. Is each one fine as it is, or worth a second thought?"
  options: ["Fine as it is", "Worth a second thought"]
  items:
    - ["Plays a puzzle game and gets a new high score", "Fine as it is", "A score says very little about Kai."]
    - ["Searches for pancake recipes", "Fine as it is", "Searches are recorded, but this one is harmless."]
    - ["Sends Nan a message to say thank you for the birthday card", "Fine as it is", "A kind message to someone Kai knows."]
    - ["Posts a photo of the front of the house with the street sign in it", "Worth a second thought", "It shows where Kai lives. Who could see it?"]
    - ["Shares a photo of a friend tripping over, without asking", "Worth a second thought", "It is about someone else. Would they want it shared?"]
    - ["Turns on a setting that shows friends where Kai is all day", "Worth a second thought", "It shows where Kai is right now, to everyone on the list."]
```

Was your guess right? Most of the trail is fine. The things worth a second thought were **hard to take back**, said **where Kai is**, or were **about someone else**.

## Explain: three questions before you add to the trail

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Three questions name what the sort showed. The planted mistake is believing that deleting takes a post back."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#mia"
      text: "Mia is in a hurry. Click the line where her thinking first goes wrong."
      answer: 2
      fault: logic
      misconception: delete-takes-it-back
      explain: "Line 2: Mia thinks she can delete it later if it is a problem. By then others may have seen, saved or passed it on. The time to think is before posting."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which question helps most before posting a photo with other people in it?"
      options: ["Would they be happy for this to be shared?", "Will it get lots of likes?", "Is my phone charged?", "Is it a good photo?"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Likes don't tell you whether it is fair to the people in it.", "That does not change who can see it.", "A good photo can still be one someone does not want shared."]
      explain: "When a post is about someone else, it is partly theirs. Ask first."
```

Three questions help before you add something to your trail:

1. **Can I take it back?** Once others have seen it, it may be saved or passed on.
2. **Does it say where I am?** A street sign, a school uniform or a live location can.
3. **Is it about someone else?** Then ask them first.

You do not need to worry about every game score or recipe search. A trail is something to notice, not something to fear. How computers work has a lesson on everything apps record, even what you never type: [Your digital footprint](../../../systems/cyber/footprint/).

## Elaborate: older trails

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Years 7 and 8: bigger audiences and longer trails, the same three questions."
check:
  type: sort
  q: "Kai is in Year 8 now. Which question matters most for each?"
  options: ["Can I take it back?", "Does it say where I am?", "Is it about someone else?"]
  items:
    - ["A voice message in a group chat of 40 people, joking about a teacher", "Can I take it back?", "Forty people can keep and forward it."]
    - ["A photo at the bus stop every morning at the same time", "Does it say where I am?", "Together, the photos show a routine."]
    - ["A video of a friend singing badly at a sleepover", "Is it about someone else?", "It is their moment. Ask first."]
    - ["A username with a full name and birth year in it", "Can I take it back?", "It is on everything that username touches, for as long as it is used."]
```

## Evaluate: a private think

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I can name the three questions to ask before I add something to my trail." }
```

**A private think** (you do not need to write it down or tell anyone): is there one thing you would ask yourself before you post next time?

```teacher
summary: "Students sort a made-up student's Saturday online into things that are
  fine and things worth a second thought, then name three questions to ask
  before adding to their trail: can I take it back, does it say where I am, and
  is it about someone else. Typical width (Years 7 and 8): bigger audiences and
  longer trails."
time: 35
timing: Engage and Explore 10 min · Explain 10 min · Elaborate 8 min · Evaluate 7 min
goals:
  - I can say why something I delete may not be gone.
  - I can name three questions to ask before I post.
  - I can tell an ordinary trail from something worth a second thought.
struggle: "Students swing to fear (everything is dangerous) or shrug (nothing
  matters). Keep coming back to the sort: most of Kai's day was fine, and three
  questions find the rest."
before: >
  **⚑ Wellbeing review:** this course is a draft. Share this lesson and these
  notes with the school's wellbeing lead before teaching, and agree the support
  pathway and any local wording.


  **If a student discloses something:** follow the school's child-protection
  procedure. Listen, don't probe, don't promise to keep it secret, and pass it
  on as the procedure says. Thank them and steer the class back to Kai.


  **Ground rules:** Kai and Mia are made up. Don't ask students what they post,
  which apps they use or what has happened to them. The closing think is
  private: not written, collected or shared.


  The one idea: a trail is normal; three questions find the parts worth a second
  thought. No laws or age rules are stated; for current rules point to the
  eSafety Commissioner (esafety.gov.au).


  Years 5 and 6: give the link with `?width=minimum` to hide the Year 8 sort.
  How computers work › Your digital footprint (Years 7 and 8) goes deeper on
  what apps collect.
running:
  - "Engage: take a show of hands on the prediction; don't settle it yet."
  - "Explore: ask why the street sign and the friend's photo were different from
    the recipe search."
  - "Explain: read Mia's lines aloud; ask where she could have stopped."
  - "Elaborate (Years 7 and 8): ask which question was hardest to pick."
  - "Evaluate: give a quiet minute for the private think; collect nothing."
stuck:
  - see: A student marks everything as worth a second thought.
    ask: What could go wrong with a pancake search?
    fix: "Most of a trail is fine. Look for the three things: hard to take back,
      where you are, someone else."
  - see: A student says deleting fixes it.
    ask: Who saw it before it was deleted?
    fix: Delete takes it off your screen, not out of everyone's memory or phone.
  - see: A student starts telling a story about something that happened to them or a
      friend.
    ask: (Don't probe.) Thank them, and bring it back to Kai.
    fix: Follow up privately if needed, and through the wellbeing team or the
      child-protection procedure if it is a disclosure.
stretch: Write a fourth question you would add to the three, and an example
  where it matters.
support: "Three cards on the desk: Take back? Where? Someone else? Hold one up
  for each item in the sort."
leads: >
  Next: who can see this? The same post reaches different people depending on
  where it goes and the settings.


  Links: How computers work › Your digital footprint (what apps collect without
  being told).
exit:
  q: Name one of the three questions to ask before you post.
  a: Can I take it back? Does it say where I am? Is it about someone else?
explain: >
  Almost everything you do online leaves a **trail**. Most of it is fine.


  Before you add something, ask three questions: **Can I take it back?** **Does
  it say where I am?** **Is it about someone else?**


  Deleting something takes it off your screen. People who already saw it may
  have saved it.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: "Kai's dog photo was deleted after a minute. Two people had already saved it.
      Whose job was it to think first: Kai's, or the people who saved it?"
    prompts:
      - What could Kai have done before posting?
      - What could the people who saved it do now?
    notes: Both. The poster can pause; the viewers can choose not to keep or pass
      things on. Keep it about Kai, not about students' own chats.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Stand on the line
      minutes: 3
      do: >
        One end of the room is "gone for good", the other is "still around".
        Stand where you think Kai's deleted photo is.
      notes: Ask a few students at each end why. Don't settle it until the Explore
        step.
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: Where could Mia stop?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Read Mia's four lines. Point to the line where a pause would have
        changed what happened. What would she ask herself?
      notes: Line 2 is where the thinking goes wrong; line 3 is where asking Jo would
        have helped.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which question?
      type: question
      q: A photo of your team in uniform, with the school's name on it. Which question
        matters most?
      options:
        - Does it say where I am?
        - Can I take it back?
        - Is it a good photo?
      answer: 0
      explain: The uniform and the school's name say where you are most days. The team
        is in it too, so ask them as well.
```

# Mia's thinking for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the line, nothing runs.

# region: mia
Mia takes a silly photo of her friend Jo at lunch.
She thinks: I'll post it now, and if it's a problem I'll delete it later.
She posts it to the class group chat without asking Jo.
Ten minutes later Jo asks her to take it down. Mia deletes it, but two people have already saved it.
# endregion
